peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the Editors and the Reviewers for their careful review of our manuscript, their comments, input, and suggestions. We are grateful for all the positive comments from the Reviewers. Below, we provide a point-by-point response to all comments. We believe that the modifications to address the comments of our reviewers have further enhanced the impact of our study.

Specific points provided by the reviewers are highlighted in italic font and any text edits to the manuscript are provided in blue Times New Roman font. In our submission, we provide two versions of our Main and Supplementary files; one in which all changes are tracked and another one in which all changes are accepted. Page and line numbers align with the tracked changes manuscript version. Table and figure numbers have been updated throughout to reflect new additions.

Reviewer 1
The first reviewer summarized the study describing “The study presents a comprehensive bioinformatics approach to investigating DNA methylation (DNAm) in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) brains, with a particular focus on regional CpG methylation (rCpGm) and its association with tau-related pathology. The authors introduce a novel rCpGm method to improve biological relevance by grouping CpGm sites based on chromatin state annotations. The integration of epigenomic and transcriptomic data provides significant insights into the role of oligodendrocyte dysfunction in AD.

The bioinformatics analysis presented in this study is innovative, methodologically sound, and supported by robust statistical validation. The novel rCpGm method offers improved biological interpretability, and the integration of multi-omic data provides valuable insights into the role of DNA methylation in AD. However, addressing the concerns outlined below—particularly regarding cell-type specificity, causal inference, batch effects, and methodological reproducibility—would further strengthen the study’s impact and applicability.”
We thank the reviewer for their evaluation of our study, positive comments and suggestions for further improvement.
The reviewer has noted two major concerns (1.1 and 1.2) and four minor concerns (1.3-1.6) to which we have responded as detailed below.

1.1. The reviewer comments on the “Cell-Type Specificity of Methylation Signals” stating “Given that bulk tissue methylation data were used, the primary conclusions regarding oligodendrocyte involvement may be influenced by cell composition effects. While adjustments for neuronal proportions were performed, additional validation using reference-free deconvolution methods (e.g., CIBERSORT, Epigenetic Clock models) or single-cell methylation data would provide greater confidence that the observed rCpGm associations are not confounded by cellular heterogeneity. The authors should clarify whether such methods were considered or could be integrated into future analyses.”
We agree that the methylation signals could be impacted by cell type composition, which is why, as the reviewer notes, we performed sensitivity analyses of our top hits adjusting for estimated neuronal proportions. As we identified a potential oligodendrocyte specific signal, we have also now adjusted for estimated oligodendrocyte cell proportions in our top hits. Using the same methods described in our Methods section, we estimated oligodendrocyte proportions by leveraging the bulk gene expression data and DSA deconvolution1 using the top 100 BRETIGEA2 cell type markers for oligodendrocytes. Similar to our neuronal proportion adjustments, we included oligodendrocyte proportion estimates in our main model (rCpGm ~ Phenotype + Age at Death + Sex + genetic PC1-3 + Oligodendrocyte proportion estimates), finding highly consistent test statistics suggesting that our findings are unlikely to be due to differences in oligodendrocyte proportions (Rebuttal Figure 1).

Rebuttal Figure 1: Comparison of Primary EWAS model results with EWAS model results adjusting for estimated oligodendrocyte proportions for all FDR significant TCX rCpGm associations. Comparison of test statistics (estimates and p-values) for all FDR significant rCpGm associations from the primary rCpGm EWAS models and models adjusting for oligodendrocyte proportion estimates. To test the correlation between estimates and p-values, we combined top hits from all phenotypes and performed Spearman’s rank correlation tests which are reported at the top of each panel. Primary model statistics are the x-axes, sensitivity model statistics are the y- axes. Green dashed line is the –log10(p-value = 0.05) value.
We have included Rebuttal Figure 1 as a new panel (D) in Figure S5 along with the other sensitivity model comparisons.
We have also edited the text as follows:
Results text on page 14 was changed from: “To ensure that these FDR significant rCpGm associations are robust to any biological and technical variations, we repeated these analyses after further adjustments for Braak stage and Thal phase, neuronal cell type proportion estimates, and sequencing batch.” To:
“To ensure that these FDR significant rCpGm associations are robust to any biological and technical variations, we repeated these analyses after further adjustments for Braak stage and Thal phase, neuronal cell type proportion estimates, oligodendrocyte cell type proportion estimates, and sequencing batch.”
Methods text on page 41 from: “Neuronal cell type proportions were estimated from the bulk tissue RNAseq data using the Digital Sorting Algorithm (DSA)1 via the DSA R package (v1.0).” To:
“Neuronal and oligodendrocyte cell type proportions were estimated from the bulk tissue RNAseq data using the Digital Sorting Algorithm (DSA)1 via the DSA R package (v1.0).”
Methods text on page 44 from: “We performed post-hoc sensitivity analyses to test the robustness of the top associations to effects of batch, neuropathological changes, and neuronal cell type proportions.” To:
“We performed post-hoc sensitivity analyses to test the robustness of the top associations to effects of batch, neuropathological changes, neuronal and oligodendrocyte cell type proportions.”
We also added the following sentence to the Methods on page 44:
“To determine if top associations were influenced by oligodendrocyte cell type proportions, we included DSA estimated oligodendrocyte cell type proportions as a fixed-effect covariate in the linear regression model: rCpGm ~ Endophenotype + Age at death + Sex + Genetic PCs 1-3 + Oligodendrocyte Cell Proportion.”
Additionally, we investigated the association between the 15 oligodendrocyte-tau-related rCpGms and total tau and pTau adjusting for the estimated oligodendrocyte proportions (Rebuttal Table 1) finding largely the same test statistics.

Rebuttal Table 1: Association of 15 oligodendrocyte- tau-related rCpGms with pTau and total tau levels from our primary model and a model adjusting for estimated oligodendrocyte proportions.

Aligning with the reviewer’s suggestion, we also investigated the 15 rCpGms of interest in cell type sorted DNAm data generated by Gasparoni et al 20183. Gasparoni and colleagues sorted 31 occipital cortex tissue samples provided by the Neurobiobank Munich using NeuN immunolabeling followed by fluorescence associated cell sorting (FACS) obtaining a neuronal nuclei population (NeuN+) and a non-neuronal/glial population (NeuN-). We downloaded the available raw Illumina 450K IDAT files from GEO (GSE66351) and processed these independently for each cell type population as described in our Methods for the Brains for Dementia Research (BDR), ROSMAP, and Weber et al 2018 datasets. We obtained a final quality-controlled dataset that included 26 glial samples (13 AD, 11 controls, 2 other) with 137,186 rCpGms and 27 neuronal samples (13 AD, 12 controls, 2 other) with 137,169 rCpGms (Rebuttal Table 2).

Rebuttal Table 2: Demographics of Replication Dataset. Summary demographics of the Gasparoni et al. 2018 sorted cell-type dataset post-quality control.

Of our 15 oligodendrocyte-tau-related rCpGms of interest, 14 were measured in this dataset. Association models between ADs vs Controls were run using mixed-effect linear regression models adjusting for age at death and sex as fixed effects and slide as a random effect variable in the glial and neuronal cell-type populations. We found that all but one of our rCpGms of interest in the glial cell population positively associated with AD matching what we expect based on our own data while only 6 out of the 14 rCpGms in the neuronal cell population positively associated with AD (Rebuttal Figure 2). While none reached a nominal statistical significance likely owing to the very small sample size of this sorted cell-type methylation dataset, there are three rCpGms with a trending association level (p-value < 0.07) in the glial enriched population with consistent direction of effect as our study (SOX8, KLK6 rCpGms). In addition, the regression estimates of the glial enriched population are larger in magnitude than the neuronal enriched populations which parallel previous evidence that AD-related DNAm associations are likely a result of changes in non-neuronal rather than neuronal populations4. Together, these results suggest that the rCpGm associations we have identified in our dataset likely originates from the glial cells which largely consists of oligodendrocytes rather than the neuronal cells.

Rebuttal Figure 2: Association of AD diagnosis with 15 oligodendrocyte-related rCpGms of interest in Illumina 450k DNAm data derived from glial (NeuN-) and neuronal (NeuN+) enriched occipital cortex nuclei populations from Gasparoni et al. 2018. After quality control, there were 13 AD and 11 Control NeuN- samples and 13 AD and 12 Control NeuN+ samples. Within each tile is the regression estimate (top) and p-value (bottom) labeled with ‘^’ if the p-value is < 0.1. Tiles are colored by regression estimate direction where red is a positive association with AD diagnosis and blue is a negative association.
We included Rebuttal Figure 2 in the supplemental figures as Figure S11 and Rebuttal Table 2 in the supplemental tables within Table S3. We have also included the following text in the Results section on page 21-22:
“Further investigation of the 15 rCpGms in Illumina 450k DNAm data derived from NeuN+ and NeuN- sorted occipital cortex nuclei3, revealed 14 rCpGms with positive associations with AD in the glia enriched NeuN- population while only 6 rCpGms had positive associations with AD in the neuronal enriched NeuN+ population (Figure S11). The regression estimate magnitudes of the glia enriched NeuN- population were also larger than the NeuN+ population suggesting that the associations identified in the bulk DNAm data are likely originating from DNAm changes in the glial cells rather than neuronal cells4.”
We also included Methods text describing the quality control and analyses for these new results as follows:
Page 45: “Sorted nuclei data from Gasparoni et al. 20183 was downloaded from GEO (GSE66351) on January 31st, 2023 for 31 occipital cortex samples using the Illumina HumanMethylation450 BeadChip.”
Page 46: “For the Gasparoni sorted dataset, ADs were defined as having a Braak stage ≥ 4 and defined as AD by the original study while controls were defined as those with a Braak stage ≤ 3 and defined as a control by the original study3.”
Page 47: “For the Gasparoni sorted dataset, EWAS were run using lmer and linear mixed models for AD diagnosis adjusting for age at death and sex as fixed effects as well as slide as a random effect.”
Lastly, although the sorted nuclei population generated by Shireby et al 20224 is not publicly available, to the best of our knowledge, the authors did make available the estimated NeuN+, SOX10+, and NeuN-/SOX- cell type proportions for their bulk DNAm data. Shireby and colleagues used their sorted DNAm data as a reference and the Houseman5 method incorporated in the R package minfi6,7 to deconvolve cell proportions from the bulk dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) and occipital cortex (OCC) data. Using these cell type proportion estimates, we investigated how further adjusting for Neuronal (NeuN+) and Oligodendrocyte (SOX10+) estimated proportions would impact the results of our BDR association models. We compared test statistics from our primary model (rCpGm ~ phenotype + age at death + sex + PC1-3 +(1|slide)) with and without bacon correction to a model that also included SOX10+ and NeuN+ cell proportion estimates for the 15 oligodendrocyte-tau related rCpGms. We found highly similar test statistics across all 3 models for each phenotype (AD diagnosis, Braak stage, and Thal phase) in the DLPFC and OCC (Rebuttal Figure 3). Using our definition for replication, even after adjustment for these estimated cell proportions, we would have still included all 15 rCpGms in downstream analyses. This is yet another piece of evidence that our findings are replicable in other datasets and unlikely to be a consequence of changes in cell proportions. Rather, they reflect methylation changes predominantly occurring in oligodendrocytes and associated with tau phenotypes in AD brains.

Rebuttal Figure 3: Association of AD traits with the 15 oligodendrocyte-tau-related rCpGms of interest in the BDR dataset with and without adjustment for estimated NeuN+ and SOX10+ cell type proportions. Within each tile is the regression estimate and (p-value) colored by p-value where a dark color indicates a p-value < 0.05 and light color p-value > 0.05. Red indicates a positive association and blue a negative association. The ‘primary.bacon’ model aligns with the results analyzed in our manuscript after applying bacon while the ‘primary’ model reflects results prior to bacon adjustment, both are shown to allow for comparisons with the cell type proportion models where bacon was not applied.
To the best of our knowledge, the data generated by Gasparoni et al. is the only cell type specific dataset currently available to us from AD donors which we could investigate our rCpGms of interest. While we believe that cell type heterogeneity does not largely impact the findings we present in our manuscript, we do agree with the reviewer that future investigation of our results in cell-type specific DNAm data should be performed to fully determine the potential contributions of cell type heterogeneity. We have edited the following sentence in the Discussion on page 33 from:
“Although the associations for the top hits we identified remained even after adjusting for neuronal proportions, future single cell type specific DNAm studies, particularly those from glial cell types4, will be important in parsing out potential cell type specific rCpGm effects in these associations.” To:
“Although the associations for the top hits we identified remained even after adjusting for neuronal or oligodendrocyte proportions and showed consistent and larger magnitude associations in glial enriched nuclei, future single cell type specific DNAm studies, particularly those from glial cell types4, will be important in parsing out potential cell type specific rCpGm effects or the role of cellular heterogeneity in these associations.”

1.2. The reviewer further comments on “Causal Relationship Between Methylation and Gene Expression” that “The study demonstrates strong correlations between rCpGm and gene expression, particularly in oligodendrocyte-related genes. However, correlation does not imply causation. While the authors acknowledge this limitation, causal inference methods such as Mendelian Randomization, Bayesian networks, or mediation analyses could help determine whether DNAm changes drive gene expression alterations or vice versa. Implementing these approaches would further substantiate the functional role of methylation in regulating AD-related gene expression changes.”
We thank the reviewer for their suggestion to more formally investigate causation. First, we applied the Mendelian Randomization (MR) approach using SNPs identified through our mQTL as instrumental variables (IV). Of the 15 tau-oligodendrocyte-related rCpGms we identified, only 4 rCpGms significantly associated (FDR p-value ≤ 0.05) with nearby genetic variants and so could be leveraged for MR. These SNPs included 92 associated with the MBP-related rCpGm, 3 with RTKN, 3 with ST18, and 1 with KLK6. As IVs need to be independent of each other to meet MR assumptions, we used PLINK28 to clump these 99 SNPs defined by linkage disequilibrium (R2 < 0.2) resulting in 8 independent loci, 4 with the MBP-related rCpGm, 2 with RTKN, 1 with ST18, and 1 with KLK6 (Rebuttal Table 3). We next tested the prediction ability of each IV SNP set for their respective rCpGm by including the rCpGm IV SNP set in a linear regression model, finding all F-statistics were greater than the suggested threshold of ten9 (Rebuttal Table 3). We also investigated if the 8 independent SNPs associated with expression of their related gene, finding no significant associations (p-value > 0.05). Together, the F-statistic and lack of association to gene expression suggest that these IV sets are valid for MR testing.

Rebuttal Table 3: SNPs used for Mendelian Randomization as Instrumental Variables.

Next, we performed an MR analysis using the TwoSampleMR10 R package to investigate if there is evidence that these four rCpGms may cause changes in expression of their related genes. For each of the 4 rCpGms, we did not find significant evidence of causation (p-value > 0.05) (Rebuttal Table 4).

Rebuttal Table 4: Mendelian Randomization results for rCpGms causing changes in related gene expression.

While these MR results do not support causation between the 4 rCpGms and related gene expression levels which were testable, it is important to note that our ability to detect a causal relationship through MR is dependent upon the prediction strength of the IV to the exposure (rCpGm), validity of MR assumptions, and statistical power. While all IV sets had an F-statistic > 10, this does not definitively confirm an IV is strong but rather indicates that the IV may be of sufficient strength as bias has been reduced to an acceptable level11. Additionally, the power of an MR test depends on sample size and the proportion of variance in the exposure that the IV explains12. The IV sets we were able to investigate overall explained a small proportion of variance in the rCpGms (3% - 9.4%, Rebuttal Table 3). This suggests that while the SNPs have predictive ability, there may not be enough power to detect a causal association with these IVs as MR studies typically require thousands of samples to detect evidence of causation. This is supported by a power analysis which revealed that we likely lack power to detect a significant MR signal in our dataset of 455 samples because if the true magnitude of association between MBP and related rCpGm was at the highest end of the 95% confidence interval (CI) (β = -0.98), we would need 694 samples to have 80% power to identify a causal association (Rebuttal Table 5). More than likely, the true magnitude of association at the MBP locus is somewhere in between the 95% CI and if it was closer to the magnitude estimated by our model (β = -0.72), a sample size > 1,200 would be required. This is similarly true for the other three testable loci as well where we would need a sample size >1,000 to have 80% power to identify causal evidence (Rebuttal Table 5).

Rebuttal Table 5: Power calculation for Mendelian Randomization of rCpGms causing gene expression changes.

Furthermore, a key assumption for MR is that the IVs are independent of confounders related to the exposure and outcome as well as the outcome itself, in this case gene expression. While the IV SNPs do not associate, even nominally, with expression levels of our genes of interest, pTau , total tau , nor AD diagnosis14, we cannot rule out the possibility that unknown confounders are influencing this relationship invalidating the IVs.
As a result, we next performed mediation analysis to determine if there was evidence of causal mediation between the oligodendrocyte-tau-related rCpGms, oligodendrocyte gene expression and pTau or total tau . We performed two types of mediation analyses using the mediation15 R package, one testing if gene expression mediates the association between rCpGm and tau (Rebuttal Figure 4A), and the second testing if rCpGm mediates the association between tau and gene expression (Rebuttal Figure 4B).

Rebuttal Figure 4: Diagram of causal mediation schemes tested. (X) is the exposure variable, (M) is the mediator, and (Y) is the outcome variable. GE = Gene expression
Prior to performing mediation, we standardized through z-score transformation the rCpGm and gene expression levels to allow for comparisons of the mediation test statistics. Tau measures were already standardized. We adjusted for age at death and sex in all input linear regression results and estimated confidence intervals through bias-corrected and accelerated (bca) bootstrapping with 1,000 simulations. We also performed sensitivity analyses including estimating how robust these associations would be to different types of unmeasured confounders.
In our first analysis (Rebuttal Figure 4A), we evaluated 32 mediation schemes for the 16 oligodendrocyte-tau-related rCpGm-gene pairs with pTau and total tau of which, 7 showed statistically significant mediation effects (p-value ≤ 0.05). These included the KLK6, ST18, CDK18, CLMN, MBP, and CD22 rCpGm-gene pairs with pTau and CD22 with total tau with a significant proportion mediated (p-value ≤ 0.05) ranging from 7% to 24% suggesting these may reflect partial mediation (Rebuttal Table 6). In our second mediation scheme (Rebuttal Figure 4B), while all 32 schemes met modern requirements of mediation, only 13 met previous requirements that the total effect of X on Y needs to be significant. Because we have good theoretical basis for this scheme, we used the modern requirements finding 31 schemes showed statistically significant mediation effects with 12 of these having a significant proportion mediated ranging from 15% to 50%. These included the KLK6, CDK18, LDB3, CLMN, MBP, and CD22 rCpGm-gene pairs with pTau and CDK18, LDB3, CLMN, MBP, and CD22 with total tau. Next, we performed sensitivity analyses finding there were no significant interactions between the mediator (M) and exposure (X) on the outcome (Y). We additionally assessed the robustness of the average mediated and direct effects to unmeasured confounders through the medsens function finding that although the direct effects are often more robust to unmeasured confounders, the mediated effects are more likely to be affected by unmeasured confounders16,17 (Rebuttal Tables 8 and 9).

Rebuttal Table 6: Mediation Results for scheme A (Rebuttal Figure 4A).
Rebuttal Table 7: Mediation Results for scheme B (Rebuttal Figure 4B).
Rebuttal Table 8: Sensitivity results for mediation analyses performed for scheme A.
Rebuttal Table 9: Sensitivity results for mediation analyses performed for scheme B.

Given that many of the mediated effects we identified were significant in both scheme A and B, we hesitate to draw conclusions of causation from this analysis. First, while we adjust for common confounders like age at death and sex, we cannot entirely rule out the possibility of unmeasured confounders which our sensitivity analyses suggest the mediated effect estimates would be sensitive to. Second, while casual mediation analysis is helpful in cases where the data is from a randomized-control trial, is longitudinal, or there is definitive knowledge about temporal ordering like genetic variants (for the most part) being fixed at birth, our data is cross-sectional where temporal ordering is not definitive. In cases where temporal ordering is not definitive, causal mediation analysis is not able to reveal whether a certain temporal order is true over another and its application is ill-advised18-20.
Taken together, we are not able to definitively determine a causal relationship between the identified rCpGms and expression of nearby genes. While previous literature does support this is a likely relationship (i.e. methylation changes lead to gene expression changes), the only definitive way to conclude that these rCpGms are causing changes in expression of nearby genes is to functionally test these through experimentation.
As a result, we have included the following text in the Results section on page 24:

Of these, there were 1,628 associations that were common and significant in both methods (Rebuttal Table 10), including 1,336 with total tau , 288 with pTau , and 4 with APOE . We further investigated if the 93 rCpGms we found to be significantly associated with both total tau and pTau and that showed replication in at least one of the BDR or ROSMAP datasets were identified by comb-p as these are high confidence, replicated associations. We found 33/93 regions (35%) were identified in both the total tau and pTau comb-p analyses including an additional 7 with pTau alone (40 total) and additional 24 with total tau alone (57 total).
Lastly, we investigated the 15 oligodendrocyte-tau-related rCpGms we identified. Of these 15 rCpGms, eight were present in the comb-p pTau and 13 with total tau analyses, of which only six (40%) were associated with both tau measures. These six included the rCpGms related to expression of the CDK18, TGFA, RTKN, two with SOX8, and MBP genes.
While we identified similar patterns of associations across measures, it is important to note that there are major weaknesses to the comb-p method when compared to our novel rCpGm method. First, comb-p does not take into account direction of effect when determining significant regions which allows individual CpGs with different effect directions to be grouped into the same region. We found that 6.6% of our comb-p associations had individual CpGms with opposing effect directions grouped into the same region. Comp-p’s lack of accounting for effect direction therefore requires the investigator to perform additional interrogation of significant regions. Moreover, because comb-p does not account for effect direction, biologically meaningful comparisons of effect direction, as we have done with our rCpGm data, cannot be conducted for comb-p regions of association.
For the purpose of comparing comb-p with our rCpGm results, we defined positive and negative comb-p associations by the effect direction for the majority of the individual CpGs making up that region. Some of the comb-p regions with discordant underlying CpGms had a slim difference in the proportion of CpGs with opposing effect direction. Thus, lack of having a direction of effect can lead to relatively arbitrary assignment of direction, again reducing biological relevance. Additionally, comb-p does not determine the magnitude of effect which limits the interpretations and conclusions that can be drawn using this method. Importantly, comb-p does not incorporate data from every CpGm within a region, but rather it only includes CpGms within a region that collectively pass a significance threshold. Defining regions through this method potentially allows for the overemphasis of some CpGm’s contributions to an association while completely ignoring others. Of the 2,362 significant comb-p regional methylation associations, 255 had between 1 to 125 CpGs (average = 10.9) within the defined regional window that were not incorporated in the comb-p results.
Another limitation of comb-p is that its CpGm grouping is not based on any biological scaffold, but rather based on arbitrarily defined windows and statistical thresholds. This poses a significant drawback when comparing associations of the same methylation data with different phenotypes from the same cohort or when conducting comparisons of different methylation datasets. Comb-p neither identifies biologically based regional associations nor enables a head-to-head comparison of the same regional associations. In contrast, our rCpGm method groups CpGms into regions based on biological definitions. Hence, by using our rCpGm method, the exact same region of CpGms is tested across phenotypes and even across different methylation datasets. Thus, our rCpGm method enables testing of biologically meaningful regions yielding results that can be directly compared and interpreted in the same manner across datasets.
In summary, results of our comparison suggest that comb-p identified associations detected by our rCpGm method, especially for total tau and pTau associations. However, our rCpGm method has numerous strengths over this method as follows: rCpGm improves the detection of regional signals across EWAS, has many more unique associations including those that replicate in additional, independent datasets, takes into account all CpGms within a region, and conducts biologically meaningful analyses across consistently defined methylation regions thereby enabling a direct head-to-head comparison of results across datasets.

We did not account for participant in our QC procedures because we performed QC separately for the TCX and CER samples such that there were no samples from the same individual in the same QC workflow. We also did not account for participant in downstream analyses because we performed our association tests for the TCX and CER data separately. As such, we did not have any donors with DNAm measures from multiple samples in the same analysis.
To address relatedness, we leveraged relatedness estimates from our previous genetic studies34,35 investigating genotype data from the same individuals used in this study. Briefly, we evaluated relatedness via the identity by descent (IBD) function in PLINK (-genome) using all independent autosomal genetic variants pruned on linkage disequilibrium (r2 > 0.8). Related pairs were defined as those with a PI_HAT score > 0.125 (3rd degree relatives or more) and the sample with the highest call rate was retained. This procedure was iteratively performed until no related individuals were detected. In our current study, the third step of our QC workflow removed individuals that previously failed the genome-wide association study QC metrics including the relatedness metric. This identified only two related pairs and therefore led to the exclusion of two samples from those pairs in this study.
While we considered applying regression-based correction for additional technical variables using techniques like ComBat-met, ComBat, or limma during our QC procedure, these methods require no missing values to calculate corrected values. As a result, we would need to either remove these missing values or impute them to apply these methods. While others have imputed missing data by using the average of all other values at that position or using a reference database, we hesitate to introduce unmeasured values into our dataset and were not able to find a reference suitable for our RRBS dataset of AD samples from brain tissue. In addition, methods like ComBat and limma were built for use with gene expression data. Although these methods have previously been applied to other data types like DNAm data, typically β-values are transformed into M-values before applying this method. We, on the other hand, are interested in using rCpGm values which are β-values averaged across a region rather than transformed M-values. Moreover, the authors of the limma package36 advise that the removeBatchEffect function not be used for linear modeling and that it would be better to include batch factors as variables in the linear model which we did as a sensitivity analysis for our top hits.
Lastly, for sample preparation and sequencing, we randomized all samples for brain tissue, sex, age at death, APOE-ɛ4 dose and CAA score to help prevent introduction of batch effects. Nonetheless, to further address the reviewer’s comment, we investigated the correlation of RRBS TCX sequencing batch with the total tau and pTau measures through ANOVA, and found no significant association between RRBS sequencing batch and either total tau (p-value = 0.719) or pTau (p-value = 0.86) measures (Rebuttal Figure 8). We agree that given the association results, both scenarios are likely, i.e. changes in rCpGm drive gene expression changes resulting in changes in tau levels vs. changes in tau levels drive rCpGm changes and lead to gene expression perturbations. To examine potential evidence for causation one way or the other, we first employed Mendelian Randomization (MR) analysis. As described above in reviewer point 1.2 where we test for evidence that changes in rCpGm levels cause changes in gene expression through MR, only 4 rCpGms had significant mQTL associations (FDR p-value ≤ 0.05) with nearby SNPs and could be tested with MR. Using the 8 independent genetic variants detailed in Rebuttal Table 3, we tested if rCpGms cause changes in total tau or pTau using the methodology described in point 1.2.
We found a significant MR result suggesting that changes in the MBP related rCpGm leads to changes in levels of total tau using the weighted median MR method (p-value = 0.04) and a suggestive association using the inverse weighted mean MR method (p-value = 0.056) (Rebuttal Table 12). We performed multiple sensitivity tests and found no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy (MR Egger intercept = 0.05 & p-value = 0.744) nor heterogeneity (Cochran Q statistic p-value > 0.5). Causal directionality via the Steiger test41 suggests that this is likely in the correct direction (Steiger p-value = 4.14E-08). Investigating the contributions of each SNP to the overall inverse variance weighted effect size also suggests that a single SNP is not driving this outcome (Rebuttal Figure 9).

These results suggest that genetically predicted rCpGm levels at the MBP locus may cause a reduction of total tau levels. However, although the 4 SNPs that were included in the IV had prediction ability (F-statistic > 10) and they explained ~10% of the rCpGm variance (Rebuttal Table 3), we only identified significance using the weighted median method and only suggestive significance using the inverse variance weighted method. Collectively, these results imply uncertainty in the casual signal identified and do not remain significant when accounting for multiple test corrections (0.05/2 = 0.025).
We were also not able to identify definitive evidence employing casual mediation as described in reviewer point 1.2 for the rCpGm, gene expression and tau variables. Taken together, despite conducting all suggested analyses, we are not able to confidently determine a causal direction unequivocally. We have therefore edited the text of the manuscript in multiple sections to allow for the multiple possibilities in causal direction and the need for functional experiments. These edits are described above in reviewer point 1.2.

## Abstract

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) brains have variable neuropathologic and biochemical changes. Capturing epigenetic factors associated with this variability can reveal novel biological insights into AD pathophysiology. Here, we conduct an epigenome-wide association study of DNA methylation in 472 AD brains with neuropathologic and biochemical brain protein levels core to AD pathogenesis. Using a novel regional methylation (rCpGm) approach, we identify 5478 significant associations, 99.7% of which associate with tau biochemical measures, and 93 concordant associations in external datasets. Transcriptome-methylome integration reveals enrichment in oligodendrocyte genes, including known AD risk gene BIN1, myelination genes MYRF, MBP and MAG previously implicated in AD, and novel genes like LDB3. Further characterization of these perturbations in independent AD and primary tauopathy datasets highlights consistent tau-related associations. In summary, we uncover the integrative epigenomic landscape of AD, demonstrate tau-related oligodendrocyte gene perturbations as a common potential pathomechanism across tauopathies and share findings via our Multiomic Atlas.

---

## Introduction

Amyloid beta (Aβ) plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles (NFT) are core neuropathological hallmarks of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) 1,2. The characteristic distribution and levels of these amyloid and tau hallmarks in the brain are often measured by Thal phase 3 and Braak stage 4, respectively. These core measures show high inter- and intra-individual brain variability within AD 5–8 suggesting the presence of distinct mechanisms controlling the levels and biochemical states of their underlying proteins. This is supported by our previous findings that key proteins involved in the pathophysiology of AD including Aβ, tau, and apolipoprotein E (APOE) each have unique genetic architectures that associate with their specific biochemical states and levels in the AD brain 9. Characterization of these endophenotype specific molecular mechanisms in the AD brain are important as each protein and state has potentially unique functions and consequences 10. Insoluble states of Aβ42 and Aβ40 are major components enriched in Aβ plaques in the brain parenchyma and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) deposits, respectively 6,11. CAA is a co-pathology often seen in AD characterized by amyloid deposits in the cerebral vasculature which can impair blood flow and may contribute to clinical deficits beyond AD 12–14. Insoluble states of tau, particularly hyperphosphorylated tau (pTau), are core components of NFT which are often seen after brain levels of soluble total tau rise and become hyperphosphorylated 15. Recent studies have also shown that membrane bound states of Aβ and tau correlate with clinical severity and that tau increases its propensity to fibrillize when contacting a plasma membrane 16–21. Moreover, the APOE protein which is important in transporting and processing lipids in the brain, is co-deposited in insoluble Aβ plaques and its gene harbors the largest known genetic risk factor for AD, the APOE ε4 tagging variant 22–24.

Although there has been great progress identifying risk for AD including genetic and environmental/lifestyle factors 25,26, the underlying molecular mechanisms that these risk factors act through to impact specific AD endophenotypes remains to be fully characterized. It is likely that these risk factors affect both shared and distinct mechanisms that underpin the hallmarks of AD and investigating these factors will be important in discovering the molecular underpinnings of AD. Epigenetic mechanisms are known to mediate genetic as well as environmental and lifestyle factor effects on gene expression. Previous epigenetic studies of AD found broad dysregulation of epigenetic mechanisms corresponding to transcriptomic dysregulation 27,28. A key epigenetic regulator of gene expression is DNA methylation (DNAm). Previous studies have found differential DNAm sites near known AD risk genes including BIN1, APOE, APP, ADAM10, MAPT, SPI1, TREM2 and others 29–37. DNAm changes have also been linked to AD risk, onset and progression 30–32,38,39. These results suggest that epigenetic regulation, particularly that of DNAm, may be important in modulating expression levels of known AD risk genes and thereby influencing core AD endophenotypes. Nonetheless, large scale, integrative studies have yet to investigate how dysregulation of DNAm impacts specific brain endophenotypes beyond global neuropathology levels. Identification of AD-endophenotype specific molecular perturbations is required to deconstruct the underlying pathophysiology of AD.

We hypothesize that, within the AD brain, neuropathology, levels and biochemical states of core AD-related proteins are influenced by variations in DNAm. To test this, we performed epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) using an innovate approach to analyze regional levels of DNAm (rCpGm) from the temporal cortex (TCX) and cerebellum (CER) with AD-related neuropathologic measures (Braak, Thal, and CAA) and brain biochemical levels of five proteins (APOE, Aβ40, Aβ42, tau, and pTau) (Fig. 1). Through our deep endophenotype EWAS and integrative omics approach leveraging a large cohort of neuropathologically confirmed AD cases, we identified widespread associations of DNAm with levels of distinct biochemical states of tau connected to significant dysregulation of nearby oligodendrocyte and myelin related gene expression. Interrogation of these tau related, epigenetically dysregulated oligodendrocyte genes and loci revealed concordant tau related associations across multiple independent datasets of AD and other tauopathies. Our findings suggest a key relationship between brain levels and biochemical states of tau and expression of oligodendrocyte genes regulated through DNAm perturbations. This may be a common pathomechanism across AD and other tauopathies. We broadly share our data and findings facilitated through our interactive web application, Multiomic Atlas of AD Brain Endophenotypes.

---

## Results

We analyzed levels of DNA methylation at CpG sites using reduced representation bisulfite sequencing (RRBS) from two brain regions, TCX and CER, in a dataset of neuropathologically confirmed AD donors with multiple AD-related endophenotype measurements. These endophenotypes included neuropathological variables (Braak stage, Thal phase, and CAA scores) and TCX biochemical measures of five AD-related proteins 10 (APOE, Aβ40, Aβ42, total tau, and phospho-Tau (pTau) (Thr231)) from three tissue fractions (soluble (TBS), membrane-bound (TX), and insoluble (FA)) (Fig. S1). Our study dataset consisted of 472 individuals (53% female) with CpGm measured from the TCX and a subset of 200 from the CER (Supplementary Data 1). After stringent quality control and data reduction steps, a total of 455 TCX and 191 CER samples with 1,958,174 TCX and 1,858,631 CER CpGm sites were available for downstream analytics (Supplementary Data 2, Fig. S2).

Grouping CpGm by predicted chromatin state is a biologically relevant method to investigate regional levels of DNA methylation
A commonly used EWAS approach to identify AD-related CpGm loci is to associate individual CpGm sites with a phenotype of interest. However, this individual CpGm based EWAS does not account for methylation variations at neighboring CpGm sites which are highly correlated and likely work together to have a functional effect 40–43. Currently available methods address this by grouping nearby significant individual CpGm sites into regions, however, these approaches are based on post-hoc statistical groupings which lack biological basis 44–47. In this study, we aimed to investigate CpGm on a regional level defined by the biological function of the genomic region to identify functionally relevant CpGm loci. To do this, we developed a novel method that averages CpGm sites into regions (rCpGm) based on biologically based genomic windows defined by the Roadmap Epigenomics Consortium 15-chromatin state model generated from the human temporal lobe 48, a region pertinent to our human brain dataset (Fig. 1).

First, to determine whether our novel method yields biologically consistent results, we investigated the average methylation levels of rCpGm sites grouped by brain chromatin states 48. We found that the average methylation levels for each chromatin state were highly consistent with the predicted biology of these states (Fig. 2). Quiescent, repressed, and heterochromatin annotations had higher methylation, typically associated with lower gene expression levels 49, whereas active transcription start sites (TSS), flanking TSS, and bivalent/poised TSS regions had low methylation levels. Chromatin regions that are expected to have more variability across cell types, like enhancer regions, have around 50% methylation in our bulk brain tissue rCpGm data. Our chromatin state specific rCpGm averages were also highly consistent with published whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) DNA methylation data 48 demonstrating the utility of our method for defining biologically relevant CpGm regions.

Next, we compared the average rCpGm levels between the TCX and CER brain regions for each chromatin state annotation. TCX and CER have mostly similar levels of rCpGm for each chromatin state with the largest differences in enhancer and transcription states which may reflect the distinct cell-specific epigenetic regulation of these two brain regions (Fig. 2). Investigating the 190 donors with both TCX and CER rCpGm measures, we found that average global rCpGm levels for each sample were similar between these brain regions (range: 0.27–0.34) and highly correlated in the same individual (r = 0.88–0.94, p < 2.2e-16), although TCX had consistently higher global methylation levels than CER (Fig. 2, Fig. S2).

We next explored the applicability of our novel method into two independent brain DNAm datasets measured via array technologies which are more often used in large-scale AD EWAS. These two datasets are the ROSMAP 30 (n = 686) and Brains for Dementia Research (BDR) 32 cohorts with CpGm measured from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in both datasets and also the occipital cortex (OCC) in BDR (n = 581, n = 576) (Supplementary Data 3). Quality control (QC) processing of the DNAm levels from these datasets through our array-specific pipeline resulted in 429,723 CpGm sites in ROSMAP and 747,577 CpGm sites in BDR. Using our novel rCpGm method, we identified 136,201 rCpGms in ROSMAP and 203,435 rCpGms in BDR (Fig. S3). These independent datasets are similar in the levels and patterns of their average rCpGm for each chromatin state annotation across these datasets (Fig. S3) and in comparison to our dataset (Fig. 2), despite differences in donors, brain regions, collection sites and methylation measurement methods highlighting the replicability of our novel analytic approach. These average rCpGm patterns are also consistent even when examining only those rCpGms common to all datasets (Fig. S3). Notably, the array-based rCpGms have a narrower range of values (Fig. S3) in comparison to our RRBS-based measurements, particularly on the hypomethylated end which may potentially be due to lower precision and dynamic range for the former methodology 50,51. Even within array-based datasets, we observe differences across chromatin states where 450K arrays have collectively higher rCpGm averages than the EPIC v1 array. These differences indicate potential methodology-specific impacts on absolute methylation value measurements, which are unlikely to influence our results since we analyze methylation levels within each dataset. We do not recommend comparisons of absolute rCpGm values across datasets measured with independent technologies. Further, rCpGm levels for each chromatin annotation are more similar between DLPFC and OCC regions for the BDR cohort than for the DLPFC region across BDR and ROSMAP cohorts (Fig. S3). This suggests that inter-individual differences may be greater than intra-individual brain region differences in methylation.

Collectively, these results underscore the robust and replicable rCpGm measurements obtained with our analytic approach which demonstrate the broad utility and biological relevance of our novel method.

DNA methylation associates primarily with tau related brain endophenotypes
To determine DNA methylation (DNAm) associations with AD-related endophenotypes we took two EWAS approaches, namely the more common method of individual CpGm associations and regional methylation associations using our novel method that averages CpGms into regions based on the 15-chromatin state model 48. We also compared results from our novel regional CpGm association method (rCpGm) to the published post-hoc regional aggregation comb-p method 45.

Neuropathology endophenotypes (Braak stage, Thal phase, CAA score) were available for all study donors (i.e., both TCX and CER samples), whereas brain biochemical endophenotypes (protein levels of APOE, Aβ40, Aβ42, Total tau, and pTau measured in soluble (TBS), membrane-bound (TX), and insoluble (FA) brain tissue fractions) were measured only from TCX tissue (Fig. S1). We performed EWAS of individual CpGm levels from both TCX and CER with neuropathology and those from TCX also with biochemical endophenotypes adjusting for age at death, sex, and the first 3 genetic principal components. We identified 2489 FDR significant TCX CpGm associations with 10 endophenotypes and 50 FDR significant CER CpGm associations only for Thal (Fig. S4, Supplementary Data 4, Supplementary Data 5). The majority (97%) of the FDR significant TCX CpGm associations were with tau biochemical measures (n = 2415). The most frequently associated endophenotype was Total tau with 2268 FDR significant TCX CpGms, 21 of which were also associated with pTau. The remaining FDR significant CpGms were uniquely associated with a single endophenotype. Top TCX CpGm associations for each endophenotype were located in or near the genes ACSF3 (Total tau), SLC16A1-AS1 (Total tau), YES1 (AB40), TRAPPC14 (Thal phase), HR (pTau), RGS10 (APOE), PLEKHJ1 (AB42), CIB1/GDPGP1 (APOE), ARPC1B (AB42), and UMODL1 (APOE). Interestingly, CpGms near ACSF3, SLC16A1, HR, RGS10, PLEKHJ1, ARPC1B, and UMODL1 have previously been identified in meta-analyses with Braak Stage, although for different CpGm positions 32,52. ACSF3, ARPC1B, CIB1, HR, PLEKHJ1, RSG10, UMODL1 also had nominal CpGm associations with CERAD score and Thal phase 32. Our top 5 CER CpGm associations with Thal phase were near genes ANKRD33, LINC02314, RAB30, ASIC1, and UBE2Q2. A previous meta-analyses of cortical tissue found CpGms near RAB30 and UBE2Q2 to be nominally associated with Braak stage and Thal phase, respectively 32.

Using our novel regional methylation analysis method, we performed EWAS with 116,014 TCX and 116,811 CER rCpGms with the same endophenotypes. We identified 5478 FDR significant TCX rCpGm associations for 5 endophenotypes (Total tau, pTau, pTau, APOE, Aβ42) (Fig. 3, Supplementary Data 6). There were no FDR significant TCX or CER rCpGm associations with any of the neuropathology endophenotypes (Supplementary Data 6, Supplementary Data 7). Concordant with the individual CpGm findings, the majority of the significant TCX rCpGm associations were with Total tau (n = 4424) followed by pTau (n = 1029). There were 738 rCpGms significantly associated with brain levels of both Total tau and pTau. All 738 rCpGms had opposite directions of association with Total tau and pTau, which is consistent with the negative correlation of these two endophenotypes (ρ = −0.21, p < 0.001) 10. This suggests that Total tau and pTau may have shared but opposing molecular mechanisms that impact their levels in the brain. Each FDR significant rCpGm was on average composed of 23 individual CpGm sites (range: 1–895 CpGms) indicating that most of these associations are not driven by a single CpGm but are a composite methylation measure of the region. The majority (69%) of the FDR significant TCX rCpGm associations reside in more active chromatin regions including active TSS (TssA, N=578), Flanking TssA (N=652), transcription at gene 5’ and 3’ ends (N=47), Strong transcription (N=175), weak transcription (N=707), genic enhancer (N=256) and enhancer (N=1363) annotations (Fig. 3) suggesting that these significant rCpGms may be functionally important in gene expression regulation.

To ensure that these FDR significant rCpGm associations are robust to any biological and technical variations, we repeated these analyses after further adjustments for Braak stage and Thal phase, neuronal cell type proportion estimates, oligodendrocyte cell type proportion estimates, and sequencing batch. Comparisons between the primary and further adjusted models by Pearson correlation revealed high, significant positive correlations of both the coefficient estimates (r = 0.998-0.9997) and p values (r = 0.66–0.989) (Fig. S5). We also investigated if the normal distribution assumptions were violated or if these associations were driven by outliers via a non-parametric Spearman rank correlation test. We found 99.3% (5442/5478) of the FDR significant associations also had a nominally significant (p ≤ 0.05) association in the Spearman rank test (Fig. S5). These highly consistent test statistics between our primary and adjusted models and their persistent significance in a non-parametric test demonstrate the robustness of these associations to potential biological and technical confounders.

To compare our rCpGm approach to the previously published comb-p method 45, we applied comb-p which groups proximal CpGms into regions based a sliding window approach and association significance. We identified 2362 significant associations (Sidak p ≤ 0.05) in 1833 unique regions by comb-p (Fig. S6, Supplementary Data 8). Unlike our rCpGm approach, comb-p does not take into account direction of effect when determining significant regions. Further, since comb-p defines regions based on arbitrary windows and statistical significance, different regions are identified for each endophenotype EWAS. This hinders a direct comparison of comb-p regions across endophenotypes, a feature which is possible by our rCpGm approach. To resolve the comb-p shortcomings on effect direction and regional variability, we defined positive and negative comb-p associations by the effect direction for the majority of the individual CpGs making up that region. We considered regions across different endophenotype EWAS to be common if there was any genomic overlap between these regions. Comb-p based regional associations largely followed similar trends as the individual CpGm and rCpGm EWAS where Total tau had the highest number of significant associations (70.2%) followed by pTau (21.6%) and APOE (6.4%). Additionally, the largest overlap of significant associations between endophenotypes were for Total tau and pTau, all with opposing directions of association, consistent with rCpGm results. There were 1628 regional methylation associations common to comb-p and rCpGm, however rCpGm identified 3763 additional associations whereas comb-p uniquely identified 677 associations.

Although both the individual CpGm followed by comb-p regional grouping and our novel rCpGm analyses found the most associations with brain tau biochemical endophenotypes, there were twice as many FDR significant loci using the latter approach. Of the 2489 FDR significant individual TCX CpGms, 68% were included in at least one of the FDR significant rCpGms. Notably, 1671 individually significant CpGms were part of the 1000 rCpGms associated with Total tau, and 26 such CpGms were within 23 rCpGms associated with pTau. Taken together, our novel rCpGm approach identifies both those loci captured by the more traditional single CpGms followed by comb-p grouping but importantly also many others that are missed by the latter. This suggests that clustering CpGms based on chromatin states is both a more powerful EWAS approach and also provides biological context for these associations. Consequently, we focused our subsequent analyses on the rCpGm results and approach. Importantly, regardless of the CpGm analytic approach, most DNAm across the genome primarily associate with tau protein levels in the AD brain.

Replication of DNAm associations with tau neuropathology and other AD-related endophenotypes in independent datasets
We next sought replication of our findings in the ROSMAP 30 (n = 686) and Brains for Dementia Research (BDR) 32 (n = 581, n = 576) cohorts that have DLPFC DNAm measured with the Illumina 450K Human Methylation and both DLPFC and OCC DNAm measured with the EPICv1 850K arrays, respectively (Supplementary Data 3). Although to our knowledge there are no DNAm datasets that also have the precise brain biochemical measures of AD-related proteins available in our dataset, ROSMAP and BDR are two of the largest cohorts with both brain DNAm and AD-related endophenotypes.

We already demonstrated the broad similarities of rCpGm levels and patterns for each chromatin state annotation across these datasets and ours (Fig. S3, Fig. 2), despite the fact that the individual CpGm sites measured by their DNAm platforms are not identical. To determine whether overlapping rCpGms that are obtained from different datasets correlate with each other, we performed pairwise correlations (Fig. S7). Using DNAm levels averaged across all samples within each dataset for all rCpGms overlapping with those from the other datasets, we conducted Spearman correlations. There are strong positive correlations for DNAm levels of overlapping rCpGm sites for each pairwise dataset analysis. As expected, these correlations are strongest for BDR DLPFC and BDR OCC datasets (Spearman Coefficient = 0.996) obtained from the same brain donors, followed by BDR DLPFC and ROSMAP DLPFC that have measurements from the same brain region both using similar array technologies (Spearman Coefficient = 0.914) and BDR OCC and ROSMAP DLFPC (Spearman Coefficient = 0.918). Nonetheless, overlapping rCpGms from our RRBS-based TCX also had high correlations with those from the other array-based datasets (Spearman Coefficients: 0.74–0.828) (Fig. S7). Thus, while not identical to our DNAm measurements, rCpGms from these other AD brain cohorts could serve as replication datasets for our findings.

For replications, we focused on the 738 TCX rCpGms that are significantly associated with brain levels of both Total tau and pTau. These 738 rCpGms are high confidence both due to their FDR-significant and biologically congruent directions of associations with two brain biochemical AD endophenotypes. Of these 738 rCpGms, 600 were present in at least one of the replication datasets. Although BDR and ROSMAP did not have brain biochemical AD-related protein measurements, they both have Braak stages, which is a measure of tau pathology. To consider an rCpGm as having a biologically congruent association in the replication datasets, the direction of effect would be the same for Braak stage and pTau and opposite for Total tau. This is based on prior work 9 and positive correlations of Braak stage with pTau (Spearman correlation ρ = 0.289, pval = 3.72E-10), but negative with Total tau (Spearman correlation ρ = −0.30, pval = 6.29E-11) in our dataset (Fig. S8).

Using these criteria, 93 out of 600 tested rCpGms had nominally significant (p ≤ 0.05) and biologically congruent associations with Braak stage in BDR and/or ROSMAP (Fig. 4, Supplementary Data 9, Supplementary Data 10). Of these 93, 3 replicated in all 3 datasets (tier 1), 23 in 2 of the datasets (tier 2), and 67 in 1 of the replication datasets (tier 3). We also performed a meta-analysis of Braak stage including the RRBS-TCX, BDR-DLPFC, and ROSMAP-DLPFC datasets and found that 47 of the 93 replicated rCpGms were significant (fixed p ≤ 0.05) including all of tier 1 rCpGms, 16/23 tier 2 rCpGms, and 28/67 tier 3 rCpGms (Fig. 4, Supplementary Data 11). We further tested the association of these rCpGms with Thal phase and AD diagnosis in the replication datasets and also found biological congruence of associations across these additional AD measures (Fig. 4, Supplementary Data 9, Supplementary Data 10). In other words, rCpGms with FDR-significant negative associations with Total tau and positive associations with pTau in our dataset, had positive associations with Braak, Thal and AD diagnosis in one or more of the replication datasets and vice versa.

When we annotated these 93 rCpGms for proximal (±1 Mb) variants identified in AD genome-wide studies 53, we found that a number of them reside near known AD risk loci including JAZF1, SIGLEC11, SCIMP, KLF16, BIN1, SPI1, ABI3, ANKH, WDR12, and SIGLEC11 53 (Supplementary Data 12). Collectively, these results support independent replication of our 93 high confidence TCX rCpGms for their association with brain tau-related and other AD endophenotypes, which may also have implications for AD risk.

Tau related rCpGms associate with expression of oligodendrocyte and myelin related genes
Most of the FDR significant AD endophenotype associated rCpGms in our dataset are located in active chromatin regions (Figs. 3, 4). To further characterize the associations between these rCpGms and brain gene expression levels, we leveraged bulk CER and TCX RNAseq data from the same individuals. After RNAseq QC, we paired rCpGms to genes ±500kb from the start and end of each rCpGm yielding 1,612,499 TCX and 1,834,887 CER cis-rCpGm-gene pairs. We then tested the association between cis-rCpGm-gene expression pairs using linear regression.

We identified 12,973 TCX and 1413 CER FDR significant cis-rCpGm-gene pairs (FDR p ≤ 0.05) (Supplementary Data 13, Supplementary Data 14). Many of the significant cis-rCpGm-gene pair associations had rCpGms annotated to expression regulation terms including active TSS, flanking active TSS, and enhancer sites (51% in TCX and 32% in CER). Genes previously reported to have AD-related methylation changes nearby, including RHBDF2 30,31, IRF8 31, CCND1 31, and SPI1 32 had both FDR significant rCpGm associations with AD endophenotypes and cis-rCpGm-gene expression associations in our dataset (Supplementary Data 13, Supplementary Data 14).

To further annotate the 93 high-confidence tau and other AD-endophenotype associated rCpGms, we tested their corresponding 1464 cis-rCpGm-gene expression pairs (1225 unique genes). Many of these 93 rCpGms reside in more active chromatin regions such as Active TSS, Flasking TSS, or Enhancers, suggesting their functional consequences in gene expression (Fig. 4). Indeed, when tested for their effects on brain gene expression, these rCpGms had FDR significant associations with nearby genes measured from the same donors (Supplementary Data 12–14). There were 535 significant cis-rCpGm-gene expression associations (459 unique genes) which included previously implicated AD genes like BIN1 23,53,54, ANXA2 55,56, CDK18 55,57,58, AKAP13 59, RORA 60,61, KIFC1 62, and KLK6 63,64 (Supplementary Data 12).

To determine if this set of 459 genes, which correspond to the 93 tau-related high confidence rCpGms, implicates common pathways or cell types, we performed gene set enrichment analysis. The top three nominally enriched gene ontology terms for these genes relate to positive regulation of myelination (GO:0031643, p=3.4E-5), gliogenesis (GO:0042063, p=1.4E-4), and microtubule nucleation (GO:0007020, p=1.5E-4) (Supplementary Data 15). Consistent with these GO terms, this gene set was also enriched for oligodendrocyte marker genes. Using the top 1000 BRETIGEA 65 cell type markers genes, there were 45 oligodendrocyte genes amongst these 459 (p=9.8E-05), 11 of which were also in the top 100 BRETIGEA 65 markers (p=4.0E-05). The set top 11 oligodendrocyte marker genes with rCpGm associations are MAG, KLK6, ST18, MYRF, LDB3, MBP, CD22, TGFA, RTKN, SOX8, and CLMN. We next investigated these 11 genes and an additional gene CKD18 further in both our and external datasets. Although part of the 1000, and not the 100 top oligodendrocyte marker genes 65, CKD18 was previously implicated in tau phosphorylation including at the T231 site and tau aggregation 58,66, found contained within NFT 58, differentially expressed in TCX tissue of individuals with AD compared to controls 58, associated with AD DNAm changes 67, and helps prevent DNA damage and promotes genomic stability 68, thereby leading us to include this gene in additional analyses.

All 12 oligodendrocyte genes have negative associations of their brain expression and paired rCpGm methylation levels (Fig. 5). There were 16 rCpGm-gene expression pairs for these 12 oligodendrocyte genes and 15 unique rCpGms. All 15 rCpGms had FDR significant negative associations with Total tau and positive associations with pTau (Fig. 5). These rCpGm~tau endophenotype associations remained significant even after adjusting for oligodendrocyte cell proportion estimates (Supplementary Data 16), indicating that they are not driven by changes in proportions of oligodendrocytes in bulk brain tissue. These rCpGms had additional nominally significant associations with other AD-related endophenotypes, the most consistent of which were negative associations with APOE levels and positive associations with pTau (Fig. S9). Almost all of the individual CpGms that comprise these oligodendrocyte rCpGms have the same direction of association with Total tau or pTau as their corresponding rCpGm, although few individually reach FDR significance (Fig. S10). This again underscores the superior power of our novel and biologically relevant rCpGm in comparison to individual CpGm analysis in detecting DNAm associations.

We further evaluated the top oligodendrocyte genes with tau-related rCpGm associations using our dataset and independent studies. Within the same brain donors, TCX expression levels of these oligodendrocyte genes also had inverse directions of associations with TCX levels of Total tau and pTau. Of these 12 top oligodendrocyte genes, 5 nominally associated with both Total tau and pTau levels (CDK18, LDB3, MBP, CD22, CLMN) and 2 with pTau (KLK6, ST18) in the TCX (Fig. 5A, Supplementary Data 17). All but one of these associations (TGFA-pTau) had directions of effect that are biologically congruent with both rCpGm-tau and rCpGm-gene associations. Notably, TGFA, unlike the other marker genes, is not only expressed in oligodendrocyte cells but is also expressed in oligodendrocyte precursor cells which may underlie this discrepancy. Upon adjustment for oligodendrocyte cell proportion estimates, CDK18, MBP, and CD22 remained nominally associated with both Total tau and pTau levels with consistent effect directions (Supplementary Data 17).

Further investigation of the 15 rCpGms in Illumina 450k DNAm data derived from NeuN+ and NeuN- sorted occipital cortex nuclei 36, revealed 14 rCpGms with positive associations with AD in the glia enriched NeuN- population while only 6 rCpGms had positive associations with AD in the neuronal enriched NeuN+ population (Fig. S11). The regression estimate magnitudes of the glia enriched NeuN- population were also larger than the NeuN+ population suggesting that the associations identified in the bulk DNAm data are likely originating from DNAm changes in the glial cells rather than neuronal cells 32.

Using three independent brain bulk RNAseq datasets of AD and control brains, we next investigated the association of these top oligodendrocyte genes with Braak stage in the Mayo TCX 69, Mount Sinai BM22 70, and ROSMAP 71 datasets from the AMP-AD study 72. Expression of LDB3 was associated with Braak stage in the Mayo TCX (beta = −0.19; FDR p = 2.54E-2) and ROSMAP (beta = −0.058; FDR p = 2.52E-2) datasets with a biologically congruent negative direction of effect (Supplementary Data 18). Using AMP-AD data, MYRF and CDK18 have also been nominated as potential therapeutic targets for AD 73, providing additional support for a role of these oligodendrocyte genes in tau-related outcomes.

To determine whether these brain rCpGm-oligodendrocyte gene-tau associations are unique to AD vs. conserved across other tauopathies, we investigated available data from methylation or gene expression studies of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and Pick’s disease. Further, we analyzed oligodendrocyte cell clusters from published brain single nucleus datasets of tauopathies to establish these associations in the cell type of interest. There was one brain DNAm study conducted from the prefrontal cortex of PSP and control donors 74 to which we applied our QC, rCpGm method and conducted an EWAS of PSP risk and Braak stage (90 PSP and 66 controls) (Supplementary Data 3 and 19, Fig. 5B). We determined biologically congruent associations with Braak stage across the 12 top oligodendrocyte rCpGms that also had consistent PSP risk associations for all but three of the genes (TGFA, ST18, CDK18). This finding supports a model where rCpGm-oligodendrocyte gene-tau associations are not unique to AD but may be a shared disease mechanism across tauopathies.

We next analyzed all available single nucleus RNAseq (snRNAseq) data from sizeable brain datasets of AD and other tauopathies 75–81 to replicate the top oligodendrocyte gene expression associations with disease risk and tau endophenotypes in an oligodendrocyte cell-type specific manner. These independent snRNAseq datasets and brain regions were from Is et al. 75 (24 TCX, AD and controls), Mathys et al. (427 prefrontal cortex, AD and controls) 76, Gamache et al. (24 TCX, AD and controls) 77, Morabito et al. (18 prefrontal cortex, AD and controls) 78, Anderson et al. (15 dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, AD and controls) 79, Rexach et al. (41 insular cortex, AD, PSP, Pick’s disease and controls) 80, and Min et al. (34 TCX, PSP and controls) 81. In addition to these snRNAseq data from a total of 583 independent brain samples from multiple regions and diagnoses, Min et al. 81 also had bulk RNAseq data from 408 PSP and control TCX samples. We tested the top brain rCpGm associated oligodendrocyte genes for their oligodendrocyte-specific expression associations with risk for AD 75–80, PSP 80,81, Pick’s disease 80, tau-related (Fig. 5B) and other available endophenotypes (Fig. S12) in these datasets. Despite differences in the cohorts, brain regions and diagnoses, there was highly consistent association for oligodendrocyte-specific expression for many of these top 12 genes with these outcomes in a direction that would be expected based on the rCpGm-oligodendrocyte gene-tau associations we identified. Most of these genes had lower expression levels in AD and other tauopathies and were negatively associated with tau-endophenotypes such as Braak stage and NFT. Most consistent associations were observed for LDB3, MYRF, MBP, MAG, TGFA, and CD22 loci where the rCpGms positively associate with pTau, negatively with Total tau and brain gene expression in our data (Fig. 5A, Supplementary Data 16–18). These rCpGms associate positively with PSP risk and Braak in Weber et al. 74 DNAm data (Fig. 5B, Supplementary Data 19).

To determine whether genetic variants could account for the tau-related DNAm changes observed for these top oligodendrocyte gene related rCpGms, we performed a cis-methylation quantitative trait locus (mQTL) analysis between these rCpGms and imputed genetic variant dosages within a distance of ±500kb. There were 160 FDR significant SNP-rCpGm associations (Supplementary Data 20). The rCpGms implicated by the mQTL associated with ST18 (14 SNP-rCpGm pairs), MBP (122), CLMN (2), MAG & CD22 (2), KLK6 (1), and RTKN (19) gene expression. Of these 160 unique SNPs, 13 near MBP nominally (p ≤ 0.05) associated with Total tau levels, the top 2 of which were also trending towards association (p < 0.052) with pTau levels (rs13381407, rs12457073: R2=1, D’=1) 9 (Supplementary Data 20), but none associated with AD risk 53. These results suggest that genetic variation is unlikely to account for the rCpGm-gene-tau relationships at these loci, with the possible exception of the MBP locus.

Collectively, these findings support a model for tauopathies such that with increasing brain levels of tau neuropathology, pTau, and decreasing Total tau, DNA hyper-methylation occurs in oligodendrocyte/myelin gene regions leading to reduced expression of these genes and potentially downstream oligodendrocyte dysfunction and dysmyelination (Fig. 5C). However, it is equally plausible that other untested genetic or environmental factors lead to DNA hyper-methylation, subsequently leading to downregulated myelin genes and oligodendrocyte dysfunction, culminating in brain accumulation of toxic tau forms 82.

We have compiled our findings and data in our interactive web application, Multiomic Atlas of AD Brain Endophenotypes. Our web application has the results from the following analyses: GWAS: Association between genetic variant dosages and TCX brain biochemical measures. rCpGm EWAS: Association between regional CpGm (rCpGm) levels and neuropathology or TCX brain biochemical measures. Individual CpGm EWAS: Association between individual CpGm levels and neuropathology or TCX brain biochemical measures. mQTL: Association between regional CpGm (rCpGm) levels and nearby genetic variant dosages (+/- 500kb). rCpGm to GE: Association between regional CpGm (rCpGm) levels and nearby gene expression measures, where rCpGms were tested for association with genes +/- 500kb from start and end of region. These data can be searched by gene names or chromosomal locations, and results are presented as both tables and interactive plots.
